task.title: Cap how much work the board does at once
task.description:
Nothing bounds how much work the board does at once. Measured on 2026-11-21 by "Review the board for use by several people at once": 300 simultaneous task creations ran 181 Git processes and slowed another reader's refresh from about 40 ms to 11 seconds; 150 simultaneous 1 MiB uploads took the server from 56 MB to 608 MB of memory. Nothing failed, but ten times that would reach the machine's process or memory limits. One signed-in person can do this to everyone.

## Decisions

Decided by Dylan on 2026-11-21.

1. 0.6.3 adds one server-wide cap on the work the board does at once, so a flood cannot exhaust the server's memory or processes.
2. Fairness between people is not solved here. The hosting guide tells whoever deploys the board to set per-person request and connection limits at the sign-in proxy. Per-person budgets are a separate backlog task.

## To settle when building

- What is capped (requests in flight, Git processes, bytes of upload held in memory, or a combination) and the defaults, chosen from measurements.
- What a request over the cap gets: a short wait and then a clear refusal with a status a client can retry on, not an unbounded queue.
- Reads the board's own refresh depends on should stay responsive while writes are saturated, as far as one cap can manage.
- Whether the cap is adjustable by an option on `workbook serve`.

## Done when

- Under a flood of simultaneous creates, uploads and reads, the number of Git processes and the server's memory stay under a stated bound, shown by a test and by a measurement against a running board.
- A request refused by the cap gets a clear answer, and the board's page shows the person something sensible rather than failing silently.
- A person's own local board behaves as it does today under ordinary use.
- `docs/reference.md` documents the cap, and gives the limits a deployment should set at its proxy.

comments.author: a@example.com
comments.body:
Dropped from 0.6.3 on 2026-11-21 (Dylan's decision) and PR #211 closed unmerged; branch feat/board-work-cap is kept at 3e4d9bcf.

What two adversarial reviews found, so the next attempt starts from it:

- First version (a cap of 16 requests, 8 writes, a line of 64): a request held its place while the client was slow, so 16 slow attachment downloads, or 8 stalled uploads, locked everyone out. main is unaffected by the same connections.
- Fix round (receive the body before taking a place, give the place back before delivering, 32 MiB budgets for held bodies and answers, pacing, 512 connections): the budgets became the weak point. About 34 connections that request a 1 MiB attachment and never read it deny every task-list read for as long as they reconnect; a task list over 32 MiB can never load; about 30 trickling uploads deny uploads for about 3 minutes a round; ten people loading a 5 MB task list at once saw 3 refused. Again main is unaffected.
- Measurements on loopback hid all of this because the operating system absorbs the answers. Test with a 1500-byte MTU (the reviewer used a Linux container) and readers with small receive buffers.
- A design that might work: cap only the board's own work, never buffer or budget answers, and when something must give, cut the slowest connection instead of refusing a new one.

The hosting guide in "Run the board behind a sign-in proxy" now says limits belong at the proxy.
